reason: The signals trace a selected stem-cell subset toward muscle precursors, the first step in building a muscle fibre.
expectation: The selected cells should develop into muscle precursors.

effect: The signals produced myoblasts that make muscle and fusion proteins, so they are ready for the fusion step.
reaction: The contrast with collagen-exporting fibroblasts makes the different cell roles clearer.
reason: The fusion proteins match the membranes of adjacent myoblasts and should help form a multinucleated fibre.
expectation: The myoblasts will fuse into a long cell with multiple nuclei.

effect: Fusion produced a multinucleated fibre with actin and myosin already in place; its covered grip sites suggest the calcium signal is next.
reaction: The distinction between one fibre and its many nuclei is clear.
reason: The calcium pulse spreads around the filaments and should enable the fibre to pull.
expectation: Calcium will expose actin's grip sites so myosin can pull the filaments.

effect: Calcium exposed the grip sites and produced sliding, so the fibre now needs calcium removed to become ready again.
reaction: The distinction between sliding filaments and shortening filaments is useful.
reason: The calcium-pumping membranes can return calcium to its internal store using ATP.
expectation: Calcium will be pumped back into storage, allowing the fibre to relax and reset.

effect: Calcium pumping stopped the pull and completed the fibre goal; the next goal is to assemble and attach both muscles.
reaction: It is useful that relaxation also requires ATP and an outside pull to lengthen the fibre.
reason: The biceps sheaths have empty spaces for muscle fibres and lead into tendons.
expectation: The fibres will fill the biceps sheaths to form a muscle with tendons.

effect: The fibres first needed extracellular connective layers to form fascicles, with enough bundles for both muscles.
reaction: I missed that intermediate step; the distinction between a fibre membrane and its connective layer is helpful.
reason: The biceps sheaths have spaces for the bundled fibres and connect them to tendons.
expectation: The fascicles will fill the biceps sheaths and form a muscle with tendons.

effect: The fascicles filled the two biceps heads, with connective tissue transmitting fibre force to the tendons.
reaction: The force pathway from fibres to tendon is a helpful connection.
reason: The biceps is assembled, but it is unclear how the remaining bundles are used to build the triceps.
expectation: The compatibility list should show what fills the triceps sheaths.

effect: The remaining fascicles automatically filled the triceps sheaths, completing the second muscle.
reaction: The different attachment routes clarify why one triceps head crosses both shoulder and elbow.
reason: The assembled biceps tendons need attachment to the movable arm skeleton.
expectation: The biceps tendons will attach across the elbow, positioning the muscle to bend it.

effect: The biceps is attached across the elbow, and the arm assembly has an empty extensor slot for the triceps.
reaction: The two poses make the biceps’ role in elbow flexion clear.
reason: The triceps is the remaining muscle and should fill the extensor slot.
expectation: The triceps will attach across the elbow opposite the biceps, enabling extension.

effect: The triceps filled the extensor slot, completing the arm and showing how attachment positions turn similar muscle pulls into opposite elbow movements.
reaction: The paired flexion and extension poses make the distinction clear.

mostWorthwhile.text: Building and resetting the fibre connected calcium, ATP and filament sliding to muscle action; the planned diagrams distinguish filaments sliding from filaments shortening.

leastWorthwhile.text: Inspecting the triceps sheaths was less informative than expected: it confirmed the remaining fascicles were compatible and immediately assembled them.

surprise.text: Relaxation requires ATP-powered calcium pumping, while an outside pull lengthens the fibre; stopping the pull alone is not depicted as lengthening it.

arbitrary.text: I initially missed the connective-tissue bundling step. The resulting fascicle illustration explains its purpose, though the term itself may be unfamiliar to students.

continue.text: I would choose to continue: connecting cellular mechanisms to the opposing movements of an assembled joint was interesting, although these are illustration plans rather than finished pictures.
